summary.title: Nobody Gets Promoted for Simplicity
summary.one_liner: Simple, well-judged engineering work goes unrecognized in interviews, design reviews and promotions, and you can make that judgment visible by documenting decisions and reframing how you and your leaders evaluate work.
takeaways: Engineers who ship the simplest working solution often get little credit, while elaborate architectures are easy to write up as promotion achievements.
Document the decision not to build something (the alternatives considered and why they were rejected) so the judgment becomes visible.
In design reviews, answer 'shouldn't we future-proof this?' by stating the cost of adding complexity later versus now, and recommending waiting.
Complexity is justified when the problem demands it (e.g., actual database limits, many teams); the issue is unearned complexity built for hypothetical futures.
Leaders can default to simplicity by asking for the simplest version to ship and the specific signals that would justify more complexity, and by recognizing engineers who delete code.
summary.summary: The author argues that engineering organizations reward complexity over simplicity across interviews, design reviews, and promotion packets, using a two-engineer example where the simpler, faster solution produces a weaker promotion narrative. He acknowledges that complexity is sometimes necessary and distinguishes earned complexity from speculative complexity. The post gives practical advice for individual engineers (describe judgment and avoided work, push back in reviews with cost analysis, talk to managers) and for engineering leaders (change review questions, scrutinize promotion packets, publicly recognize simplicity).
